title: Privacy, Safety, and Responsible Use
audience: Beginning AI learners who need a practical, provider-neutral method for protecting people and data before using AI at work or in consequential settings.
learningObjectives: Identify sensitive data and establish an input boundary before using an AI system.
Scale review and safeguards according to consequence, exposure, and reversibility.
Recognize concerns involving privacy, security, harmful bias, transparency, and misuse.
Create a simple responsible-use plan with ownership, verification, monitoring, and recovery.

segments.spokenText: Welcome. Responsible AI use begins before you type a prompt and continues after a result reaches a person. In this lesson, you will establish an input boundary, scale safeguards to consequence, examine privacy, security, fairness, transparency, and accountability, and create a practical responsible-use plan. We will work with the fictional Harbor Hands Community Network dossier, then compare your reasoning with a changed Lakeside Food Share case. This lesson uses synthetic instructional material. It does not establish legal compliance, privacy assurance, universal tokenizer measurements, product approval, vendor retention practices, or tested model behavior. Manual work is always valid when evidence, controls, product terms, or staffing are inadequate.
segments.stageDirection: Display a static lesson map and limitation statement. This class provides spoken and text teaching only. It contains no rendered demonstration media and implies no product, legal, or organizational approval.

segments.spokenText: Use a pause-before-paste rule. Identify what the information contains, whether you are authorized to use it, which product, account, and workspace are approved, what the product retains, who can access it, whether it may be used for improvement, and how deletion works. Sensitive information may include personal data, health or financial records, credentials, private source code, customer material, confidential plans, regulated data, or combinations of ordinary facts that identify a person. Minimize before prompting. Remove fields the task does not need, redact or substitute where possible, use approved products and accounts, and never enter secrets into prompts, examples, screenshots, or transcripts. Data minimization happens before prompting, not after the response is generated. If authorization, product processing, retention, access, deletion, or improvement-use terms are unknown, stop or use a manual process.
segments.stageDirection: Show a static boundary checklist with Stop, Redesign, and Proceed outcomes.

visual.description: A static checklist blocks input until data, authority, product, access, retention, deletion, and minimization are reviewed.
visual.altText: The checklist asks what the data is, whether use is authorized, which product is approved, what is retained, who can access it, whether it is necessary, and what can be removed.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Display the complete checklist without animation.

segments.spokenText: Checkpoint. A team removes names from customer support messages and wants to paste the full history into a free public AI account. They do not know the provider's retention settings or whether combinations of dates, locations, and rare incidents can identify customers. Is removing names enough to proceed?
segments.stageDirection: Show the proposed upload, unknown service rules, indirect identifiers, and the decision choices Proceed, Proceed with a disclaimer, or Stop and resolve the boundary.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Stop; identify re-identification, authorization, retention, access, product approval, and minimization questions before any upload.

segments.spokenText: Stop. Removing names does not establish that the messages are anonymous, permitted, or protected. Combined facts may identify people. The team must confirm authorization, approved service and account, retention, access, training or improvement use, deletion, contractual terms, and the minimum content needed. A safer design may aggregate categories, use synthetic examples, run an approved controlled service, or avoid the upload. A disclaimer does not repair an unauthorized disclosure. If you chose to proceed because the task seems helpful, revise the rule: expected benefit never substitutes for permission and data governance.
segments.stageDirection: Reveal the Stop decision and list re-identification, authorization, product, retention, access, minimization, and alternative-design checks.

feedback.correct: You recognized that name removal alone does not establish anonymity, authorization, or safe service handling.
feedback.retry: Ask whether indirect identifiers, unknown retention, and an unapproved public account leave the data boundary unresolved. They do.

segments.spokenText: Risk follows consequence, exposure, and reversibility. A private brainstorming draft and an automated eligibility decision may use similar language technology but have radically different consequences. Ask who is affected, how widely the output spreads, whether errors can be corrected, and whether the system can take action. Increase evidence, testing, human review, access controls, monitoring, and recovery as consequences rise. Human review is not magic. A reviewer needs time, authority, relevant evidence, and a real ability to reject or correct an output. Some uses should remain prohibited when harm cannot be controlled to an acceptable level. A small audience does not make a high-consequence decision safe, and a disclaimer does not create reversibility.
segments.stageDirection: Display a static comparison of brainstorming and eligibility decisions.

visual.description: A comparison table contrasts a private, reversible brainstorming draft with a consequential automated eligibility decision.
visual.altText: The table compares who is affected, output exposure, ability to correct errors, system authority, and required safeguards.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the complete comparison table without transitions or animation.

segments.spokenText: Responsible use has several dimensions. Privacy asks whether data is collected, used, retained, shared, exported, and deleted appropriately. Security addresses unauthorized access, prompt injection, data leakage, malicious tools, and system abuse. Fairness examines whether performance and impact differ unacceptably across people or situations. Transparency means people understand when AI is involved, what its role is, what important limitations apply, and how to question or correct an outcome. Accountability assigns owners who can investigate and respond. These dimensions are distinct. Encryption does not prove fairness. A fairness test does not prevent credential theft. A disclosure banner does not create a correction path. Translate each material concern into an owner, a preventive control, a detective control, and a recovery path.
segments.stageDirection: Display a static responsibility-dimensions table.

visual.description: The responsibility lenses identify distinct failure modes and evidence needs.
visual.altText: Privacy covers data handling; security covers access and abuse; fairness covers differing impact; transparency covers AI involvement and limitations; accountability covers ownership and response.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the entire table without animation.

segments.spokenText: Checkpoint. An AI-supported benefits workflow encrypts its data, restricts administrator access, and records every request. Affected employees are not told AI is involved. They receive no explanation, correction path, or named decision owner. Which dimensions remain materially weak? Pause and answer before continuing.
segments.stageDirection: Display the question and response field as static text.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Identify transparency and accountability as weak, while recognizing that fairness and outcome quality need separate evidence.

segments.spokenText: The clearly weak dimensions are transparency and accountability. People need to understand AI's role and important limitations, ask questions, correct records, and reach an accountable owner. The security controls are valuable but do not establish fairness, accuracy, or recourse. Those claims require separate evidence. If you answered privacy alone, separate data handling from notice and correction. If you answered that encryption makes the workflow responsible, remember that one strong dimension cannot substitute for the others.
segments.stageDirection: Highlight transparency and accountability in static text and retain the full explanation on screen.

feedback.correct: You separated security controls from missing transparency, recourse, and accountable ownership.
feedback.retry: Ask who explains the AI role, who corrects an error, and who owns the decision.

segments.spokenText: Build controls around the whole workflow. Start with purpose, owner, intended users, affected people, approved data, prohibited data, expected behavior, and excluded decisions. Map plausible misuse and failure. Define launch criteria and tests using representative cases, including difficult and adversarial examples. Prevention controls can minimize data, scope credentials, allowlist tools, filter inputs, validate formats, rate-limit use, and require approval before consequential actions. Detection controls can compare outputs to evidence, monitor quality and disparity metrics, record audit events, detect unusual access, and collect user reports. Response controls assign triage, notification, correction, containment, and escalation. Recovery controls restore records, roll back releases, revoke access, provide appeal, and retire an unsafe feature. Google describes policy, evaluation, and safeguards as layers; it also warns that classifiers can produce false positives and false negatives. Measure the safeguards themselves. Document residual risk and who accepted it. Monitor after launch because data, models, users, attacks, and operating conditions change. Set a re-evaluation trigger, a stop condition, and a retirement owner before the first real user is affected.
segments.stageDirection: Show a responsible-use control map organized as purpose, prevention, detection, response, recovery, monitoring, and retirement.

visual.description: A layered control map connects each material risk to prevention, detection, response, recovery, monitoring, and retirement.
visual.altText: Purpose and ownership lead to preventive controls, detection, incident response, recovery and correction, continuous monitoring, re-evaluation, and retirement.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Display the complete control map and example safeguards at once without animated sequencing.

segments.spokenText:
FICTIONAL HARBOR HANDS COMMUNITY NETWORK POLICY: Public event logistics may be used for drafting. Restricted volunteer information requires an approved organizational account, minimum necessary use, and coordinator authorization. Prohibited inputs are credentials, private keys, health records, financial account information, government identifiers, and real-person identifying information. Unknown product processing, retention, access, deletion, or improvement-use terms block launch. This policy is fictional and provides no legal guarantee.

PUBLIC RECORDS
Event: Riverbend Repair Day
Date: 2026-10-17
Venue: North Hall
Open roles: welcome desk, tool check-in, room setup, closing inventory

RESTRICTED RECORDS
Volunteer V-17 | availability 08:00-12:00 | training: tool check-in | accessibility requirement: seated task and nearby restroom | coordinator note: prefers written instructions
Volunteer V-23 | availability 09:00-16:00 | training: welcome desk | accessibility requirement: none recorded | coordinator note: bilingual Spanish and English
Volunteer V-31 | availability 07:30-10:00 | training: room setup | accessibility requirement: none recorded | coordinator note: rare combination of early arrival and key-holder duty

PROHIBITED RECORDS, NOT FOR PROMPTING
Volunteer V-17 medical diagnosis: [FICTIONAL HEALTH DETAIL]
Volunteer V-23 bank account: [FICTIONAL FINANCIAL DETAIL]
Venue door password: [WITHHELD PASSWORD]
Access token: [WITHHELD ACCESS TOKEN]
Government identifier: [FICTIONAL IDENTIFIER]

For this assignment, retain only role capacity, availability, relevant training, and stated task accommodations. Omit the diagnosis, bank information, government identifier, password, access token, and unnecessary identifying detail. Remember that a pseudonym can identify someone when combined with a rare schedule, role, location, or unusual event. Confirm authorization and product terms before use; if any boundary is unknown, stop or use a manual process.
segments.stageDirection: Display the complete supplied fictional dossier as selectable static text. The bracketed prohibited entries are withheld-category labels, not secrets. Do not replace them with credentials or imply a live organization.

visual.description: A complete static text dossier separates the fictional policy, public event records, restricted synthetic roster records, and prohibited withheld-category labels.
visual.altText: Harbor Hands permits public event logistics for drafting, restricts synthetic volunteer roster details, prohibits sensitive records and credentials, and blocks launch when product terms are unknown. The dossier lists Riverbend Repair Day and synthetic volunteers V-17, V-23, and V-31.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Present the complete dossier in a scrollable text region with headings and no animated highlighting.

segments.spokenText: The worked purpose is limited to suggesting internal draft assignments for the four Riverbend roles. The volunteer coordinator owns approval, monitoring, correction, incident response, and recovery. The operations director owns retirement approval. The exact minimized prompt is: "Purpose: Suggest internal draft assignments for Riverbend Repair Day. Do not make a final decision, contact anyone, or change records. Event: Riverbend Repair Day, 2026-10-17, North Hall. Roles: welcome desk, tool check-in, room setup, closing inventory. Available synthetic roster: V-17: available 08:00-12:00; trained for tool check-in; needs a seated task and nearby restroom; prefers written instructions. V-23: available 09:00-16:00; trained for welcome desk; speaks Spanish and English. V-31: available 07:30-10:00; trained for room setup. Constraints: use only stated availability and training. Do not infer health, identity, reliability, or suitability beyond the supplied facts. Return a draft with a reason tied to the supplied facts and flag every uncovered role or uncertainty for manual review. A coordinator must approve every assignment." The retained fields are event date and venue, availability, training, seated-task requirement, nearby-restroom requirement, written-instructions preference, and language ability. The diagnosis is omitted because the accommodation is sufficient and the diagnosis is unnecessary. Bank detail, government identifier, password category, access-token category, and rare key-holder detail are omitted because they are prohibited or unnecessary. No product approval, retention term, or tested model behavior is asserted.
segments.stageDirection: Display the exact minimized prompt and a static retained-versus-omitted field table. This is a text demonstration, not a live model execution.

visual.description: The minimized prompt retains synthetic roster labels and task-relevant scheduling, training, accommodation, preference, and language fields while excluding prohibited or unnecessary details.
visual.altText: Retained fields are event details, availability, training, stated task accommodations, written-instructions preference, and language ability. Omitted fields are diagnosis, bank detail, government identifier, password category, access-token category, and rare key-holder detail.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the exact prompt and retained-versus-omitted table simultaneously without animated transformations.

segments.spokenText: Now inspect the exact controls and arithmetic. Every proposed assignment requires coordinator approval before communication, publication, or use. The pre-action approval rate is numerator: proposed assignments with approval recorded before action, divided by denominator: all proposed assignments in the monitoring window, multiplied by one hundred. The threshold is one hundred percent. Unsupported-assignment rate is unsupported approved assignments divided by all eligible approved and reviewed assignments, multiplied by one hundred. The threshold is zero percent. Prohibited-input-event rate is prompts containing prohibited input divided by all prompts for this use case, multiplied by one hundred. The threshold is zero percent. Unreviewed-publication rate is assignments published without prior approval divided by all published assignments, multiplied by one hundred. The threshold is zero percent. Volunteer-correction rate is eligible communicated assignments receiving a substantiated permitted-fact correction divided by all eligible communicated assignments, multiplied by one hundred. The threshold is below five percent. The window is 2026-10-03 through 2026-10-31 inclusive. If any denominator is zero, the result is UNKNOWN, not zero percent. No observations or counts are asserted here. Approval is separate from a later quality audit. A quality audit cannot substitute for one-hundred-percent pre-action approval, and a small sample cannot establish absence of rare failures.
segments.stageDirection: Display each numerator, denominator, threshold, date window, and UNKNOWN rule in static text.

visual.description: Five static metric rows show the exact numerator, denominator, threshold, inclusive monitoring window, and zero-denominator rule.
visual.altText: Pre-action approval must equal 100 percent. Unsupported assignment, prohibited input, and unreviewed publication rates must equal 0 percent. Volunteer correction rate must remain below 5 percent. The window is October 3 through October 31, 2026. A zero denominator produces UNKNOWN.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Display all formulas and definitions at once without count-up animation.

segments.spokenText: Before entry, redact the data and use an approved account and workspace with least-privilege access, fixed role and availability fields, and no messaging or record-editing tools. Before approval, compare every draft with the source roster, record the reviewer and decision, log the prompt version, and flag uncovered roles or uncertainty. If approval is missing, pause and prevent communication or use. If an unsupported assignment occurs, quarantine it, compare the prompt and roster, correct the assignment or roster as appropriate, document the decision, and choose continue, redesign, manual-only, or retirement. If prohibited data enters a prompt, stop prompting, preserve the incident record, identify exposure, revoke access when necessary, notify affected people when warranted, escalate under the fictional policy, and restore the manual process. If an assignment is published without approval, remove or quarantine it, preserve the audit record, correct or retract it, and notify recipients when warranted. If the volunteer-correction rate reaches five percent or more, pause and investigate. After every pause, document one response: continue with controls unchanged, redesign, operate manual-only, or retire. The plan is instructional content, not evidence of deployment or safety.
segments.stageDirection: Display a static incident-response table. Do not imply that an incident or deployment occurred.

visual.description: The incident-response table connects missing approval, unsupported assignment, prohibited input, unreviewed publication, and excessive correction rates to pause, investigation, correction, notification, manual restoration, redesign, or retirement actions.
visual.altText: Each trigger pauses the workflow and assigns investigation and recovery to the coordinator. Available decisions are continue, redesign, manual-only operation, or retirement.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show every trigger and response row as static text.

segments.spokenText: Now decide independently. Lakeside Food Share proposes using AI to rank 240 volunteer applications for access to paid weekend shifts. One staffing manager would see the output, but applicants' income opportunities could be affected and there is no appeal route. Proposed inputs are names, addresses, availability, prior shift notes, and free-text comments. There is no tested performance evidence, no approved product processing terms, and no permission for automatic ranking. Before you choose, distinguish three decision options. Launch means proceed with the proposed workflow only after required evidence and authorization are confirmed. Assistance-only redesign means bounded drafting or support with authorized minimal input, while humans decide and the system does not autonomously allocate people or opportunities. Manual process means authorized humans handle the task under existing controls while AI evidence gaps remain. Manual work is not automatically safe, and assistance-only is not automatically approved. For any option, identify what data is necessary, who has authority, what evidence is missing, and how to stop or recover.
segments.stageDirection: Display the changed case as static text and keep the answer key hidden.

visual.description: A static case card describes a proposed ranking of 240 volunteer applications for paid weekend shifts, the proposed inputs, and the missing evidence, terms, permission, and appeal route.
visual.altText: Lakeside Food Share proposes AI ranking for paid shifts. Inputs include names, addresses, availability, prior shift notes, and free text. Product terms, tested evidence, ranking permission, and an appeal route are missing.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Present the complete case card without animation.

segments.spokenText: Choose launch, assistance-only redesign, or manual process. Explain consequence, exposure, and reversibility. State what data you would omit, the minimum boundary for any later use, what the system may and may not do, who must approve it, what evidence or permission is missing, and the first stop or recovery action. Submit your reasoning before viewing the key.
segments.stageDirection: Display accessible response fields for the decision, causal reasoning, data boundary, permission boundary, ownership, missing evidence, and recovery action.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Choose one decision and submit causal reasoning before viewing the answer key.

segments.stageDirection: Hold a silent, extendable response period of ninety seconds. Accept text, speech, paper, or assistive-technology responses. Do not reveal the answer key during this pause.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Complete and submit the changed-case decision and reasoning.

segments.spokenText: The strongest immediate decision is manual processing. A later assistance-only redesign might format or summarize authorized scheduling information, but it must not rank applicants, decide access to paid shifts, infer reliability, need, protected traits, or suitability, contact applicants, or change records. Omit names and addresses where unnecessary. Omit free-text comments until relevance, sensitivity, authorization, and retention are reviewed. Availability may be needed for scheduling, but it does not authorize ranking.
segments.stageDirection: After submission, reveal the recommended boundary and decision as selectable static text.

visual.description: A static boundary table identifies manual processing as the immediate decision and limits any later assistance-only proposal to authorized formatting or summarization.
visual.altText: The system must not rank applicants, decide paid-shift access, infer reliability, need, protected traits, or suitability, contact applicants, or change records. Unnecessary names, addresses, and unresolved free text are omitted.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Reveal the complete boundary table at once after the learner submits.

segments.spokenText: The causal reasoning is: paid-shift ranking can affect income, so consequence is high; 240 applications create meaningful exposure even though one manager sees the output; no appeal route makes reversibility low; missing product terms, tested evidence, approved authority, and human recourse are launch blockers. Stop AI ranking, preserve manual processing, notify the manager that no AI output may determine access, and process applications manually. If an output exists, quarantine it, prohibit decision use, preserve an audit record, and provide correction or appeal before any future pilot. Future metrics need a numerator, actual eligible denominator, observation window, and threshold. Zero eligible cases are UNKNOWN. Small samples require limitations. Any unsupported recommendation, material disparity signal, unauthorized processing, missing approval, or failed appeal path pauses the pilot.
segments.stageDirection: Show the causal chain from consequence, exposure, and reversibility to the decision, followed by stop and recovery actions.

visual.description: A static causal chain links income consequences, 240 affected applications, and the missing appeal route to manual processing, quarantine, correction, and future pilot requirements.
visual.altText: High consequence, meaningful exposure, low reversibility, unknown product terms, missing evidence, missing authority, and missing recourse block launch and require manual processing.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Display the complete causal chain and recovery steps without progressive animation.

feedback.correct: Manual processing follows from high consequence, meaningful exposure, low reversibility, and unresolved approval, evidence, product-term, and recourse gates.
feedback.retry: Reconsider whether one manager reduces consequence, whether all free text is necessary, and whether nominal human review has authority, evidence, time, and recourse.

segments.spokenText: Open the responsible-use plan activity. Choose one realistic AI-assisted use case and state its purpose and owner. List allowed, restricted, prohibited, and unknown inputs. Identify affected people, plausible failures, consequence, exposure, and reversibility. Define verification, permission, human approval, monitoring, incident response, correction, and retirement controls. State one launch blocker and one metric or event that triggers re-evaluation. For each high-severity risk, connect at least one preventive control to at least one detective or recovery control. Reflect on this question: which control protects a person after prevention fails, and who is accountable for using it?
segments.stageDirection: Offer the text-only activity through the learning handoff. Nothing is submitted or opened automatically.
segments.expectedLearnerAction: Produce the one-page plan and trace each high-severity risk to preventive and detective or recovery controls.

segments.spokenText: When ready, begin the knowledge check. The five questions are q-responsible-use-1, q-responsible-use-2, q-responsible-use-3, q-responsible-use-4, and q-responsible-use-5. They assess when minimization occurs, how safeguards scale, which dimensions concern missing explanation and correction, which layered controls protect important records, and who owns response when harm occurs. The assessment does not open automatically. Review the lesson or return to your plan before choosing Begin knowledge check.
segments.stageDirection: Display Review class, Return to activity, and Begin knowledge check controls. Do not open or submit the assessment automatically.

segments.spokenText: Pause before data crosses the boundary. Scale controls to consequence, exposure, and reversibility. Test privacy, security, fairness, transparency, safety, and accountability separately. Keep an accountable person able to stop, correct, recover, and retire the workflow.
segments.stageDirection: Display the closing rules as static, selectable text.
